1.pericope_label: And I looked, and, lo, a Lamb stood on the mount Sion, and with him an hundred forty and four thousand, having his Father’s name written in their foreheads. And I heard a voice from heaven, as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of a great thunder: and I heard the voice of harpers harping with their harps: And they sung as it were a new song before the throne, and before the four beasts, and the elders: and no man could learn that song but the hundred and forty and four thousand, which were redeemed from the earth. These are they which were not defiled with women; for they are virgins. These are they which follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth. These were redeemed from among men, being the firstfruits unto God and to the Lamb. And in their mouth was found no guile: for they are without fault before the throne of God.

schools.summary: Read the chapter as a deliberate episode of relief, since the two preceding chapters described woes threatening to destroy the church and the gloomy picture needed breaking by symbols holding out ultimate and certain victory. Press the article, that it is the Lamb and not a lamb, and set Zion against the Babylon about to be introduced — the citadel of the heavenly city against the world-city. Locate the mountain as the site of the new city of God, and note that the name on their foreheads stands exactly where the mark of the beast stood, the seal protecting them. Take the number as representing the full growth of the choice ones of God, the true Israel, and note that some scholars seek a distinction between this company and the sealed of the earlier vision, though it is better to refer them to the same. On the song, correct the rendering and probably the text, giving they sing rather than they sung as it were, and observe that in the earlier vision the new song was sung by the living creatures and the elders while here it is sung before them, apparently by the redeemed themselves; the reason none else can learn it is that no one who has not been redeemed can enter into the feelings of those who were. On the undefiled, lay out the scholarship without settling it: the noun applies to men as well as women, one commentator takes the language metaphorically as the symbolic character of the book suggests, another judges it an interpolation in the interest of celibacy, a third holds that taken literally it can refer only to adultery or fornication — and insist that since the New Testament exalts marriage the passage should not be construed as degrading it.

Take the Lamb as representing Christ in his sacrificial office and the mountain as a type of the Christian church. On the song, keep the point narrow — others could not sing and play it in the same manner. On the undefiled, read them as pure from idolatry and presented as unspotted virgins to their Saviour, with a possible allusion to Israel's sin through the Midianite women; or treat the phrase as part put for the whole, the deepest defilement standing for every other, so that virgins means unspotted souls who have preserved universal purity in soul and body alike. Say that they follow the Lamb through good and through evil report, bearing his reproach and not loving their lives to the death, and take the firstfruits of those Jews who were the first converts. On the mouth without guile, note that when brought before kings and rulers they did not dissemble but boldly confessed the Lord Jesus.

Set the two standing-places against each other: the beast stands on the sand of the sea, the Lamb on Mount Zion. When the body had been shown which was confounded by the power of the dragon and marked with his brand, the church is shown rejoicing in its wonted splendour and numbers, so that no one should fear the body of the Lamb had succumbed to the fury of the beast. Then offer an arithmetic for the number: the finite figure ought to be understood as infinite, and as suited to the virgin band which loves God from the whole heart, the whole soul and the whole mind, and to the body also, which consists of four qualities; for three times three are nine, and four times four sixteen, and sixteen times nine make one hundred and forty-four.

Work the antithesis through the animal: a counterfeit lamb had risen out of the earth in the previous chapter which was really a dragon, whereas here is the true paschal Lamb, so that his mediatorial government is the fruit of his sufferings and the cause of his people's safety and fidelity. Note that Mount Zion is the gospel church, that Christ is in the midst of her in all her troubles and therefore she is not consumed, and that it is his presence which secures her perseverance. Then observe how honourably his people appear: many, even all who are sealed, not one lost in all the tribulations through which they have gone, and bearing the name of God on their foreheads as a bold and open badge.

Identify the defilement with the whore of Rome and her harlots, so that while the kings and inhabitants of the earth were drunk with the wine of their fornication, which is spiritual fornication, these were free from such idolatrous practices. On the guile, report that several copies and all the Oriental versions read lie rather than guile, and that by a lie may be meant idolatry, since idols are often called lies and lying vanities, or else false doctrine, so that these did not speak lies in hypocrisy as the followers of antichrist do. Take the new song for the song of redeeming grace, sung by the hundred and forty-four thousand.

debates.question: Are the undefiled literally chaste, or is the language figurative?

sides.position: Literally chaste; the word for defiled determines the sense, though the passage may not be pressed further
Figuratively: they are pure from idolatry, presented as unspotted virgins to their Saviour
Part put for the whole, the deepest defilement standing for every other, so virgins means unspotted souls

Unsettled: one takes it metaphorically, another as an interpolation in the interest of celibacy, a third as covering only adultery — but the New Testament exalts marriage and this must not be read as degrading it

debates.question: Is this company the same as the sealed of the earlier vision?

sides.position: The same; some scholars seek a distinction somehow, but it is better to refer them to the one company
A number representing the full growth of the choice ones of God, the true Israel
An infinite number under a finite figure, three times three by four times four

debates.question: Why could no one else learn the song?

sides.position: Because none who had not been redeemed could enter into the feelings of those who were
Because others cannot know the communion believers hold with the Father and the Son
Only that they could not sing and play it in the same manner

outliers.note: Alone offers an arithmetic for the number, deriving a hundred and forty-four from three times three multiplied by four times four, the nine standing for wholeness of heart, soul and mind and the sixteen for the four qualities of the body.

Alone reports the state of scholarship on the undefiled instead of taking a side, naming three incompatible positions and then refusing all of them on the ground that the New Testament exalts marriage.

themes: a Lamb stood on the mount Sion
they sung as it were a new song
in their mouth was found no guile

6.pericope_label: And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people, Saying with a loud voice, Fear God, and give glory to him; for the hour of his judgment is come: and worship him that made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and the fountains of waters.

schools.summary: Take another to mean simply a further angel in a series the seer had grown used to, and read the vision's design as identical with the previous one, to sustain the courage of a persecuted church by the assurance that the gospel would ultimately triumph. Then press the wording, which is careful: this is the only occurrence of the noun for gospel anywhere in the writer's works, it stands without the article, so that what is proclaimed is not the gospel but a proclamation of God's eternal purpose, and the adjective for everlasting appears nowhere else in the book though it is common in the fourth gospel and the first epistle. Record that Origen took the eternal gospel here to be another book still to be written. Note the grammatical seam, that the participle for having agrees with the angel while the participle for saying shifts to the nominative as though a new sentence began. Or take it as the gospel outright, the good news that God loves the world and has redeemed mankind, the sword of the Spirit put into an angel's hand and raised in view of all nations. Read the summons as addressed to people sitting inactive on the earth who must be roused, call it a summons to judgment with no hope offered except by implication, and answer the question when this angel appeared by saying that the whole cycle of gospel preaching is included in the vision, though some ages have seen the light go forth with revived lustre.

Decline to choose between a dispensation of providence, an order of preachers and a society of Christians, then identify the vision with an institution of the present day, whose object is to print and circulate the Scriptures through all the habitable world and in all the languages spoken on the face of the earth; list the tongues already served. Make the three angels of this passage three men who bring messages from God, the first exhorting to the fear and worship of God, the second proclaiming the fall of Babylon, the third warning concerning the beast. Hold that this is not the gospel properly so called but a joyful message meant to have influence on all ages. Then draw the practical consequence: those who fear God and give him glory will not worship the beast nor any image whatever; and note that the four things named as made by the Creator are precisely the objects on which the vials are afterwards poured.

Observe that the gospel is everlasting in its nature and in its consequences, since all flesh is grass but the word of the Lord endures for ever; that it is work fit for an angel to preach it, such being the dignity and the difficulty, and yet we have this treasure in earthen vessels; that it concerns all the world and should therefore be made known to every nation and kindred and tongue; and that it is the great means whereby men are brought to fear God and give glory to him.

Deny that the angel is one of the ministering spirits at all, since the preaching of the gospel is committed to none of them, and take it for a set of gospel ministers rather than a single man. Canvass the candidates in order: the eighth and ninth century opponents of image worship, who called men to fear God and worship him and not images — but reject them, because little of the everlasting gospel was preached in those times; then the forerunners of the Reformation, Wycliffe in England, Petrarch in Italy, and Huss. Add that these ministers will lift up their voice like a trumpet and cry aloud, delivering the gospel fully and faithfully with great authority, vehemence and zeal.

debates.question: Who is the angel with the everlasting gospel?

sides.position: Not a ministering spirit at all, since preaching is committed to none of them, but a set of gospel ministers — perhaps the forerunners of the Reformation
Possibly a dispensation of providence, an order of preachers or a society; the vision seems descriptive of the British and Foreign Bible Society
One of three men who bring messages from God
Simply a further angel in a series, the vision's design being to sustain a persecuted church

debates.question: Is this the gospel, or a gospel?

sides.position: Not the gospel: the noun stands without the article, so what is proclaimed is a proclamation of God's eternal purpose; Origen even took it for another book still to be written
Not the gospel properly so called, but a joyful message meant to have influence on all ages
The gospel outright — the good news that God loves the world and has redeemed mankind
Everlasting in its nature and in its consequences alike
The whole cycle of gospel preaching is included in the vision, though some ages have seen the light go forth with revived lustre
In the eighth and ninth centuries, or with Wycliffe, Petrarch and Huss
In the present day, in the printing and circulation of the Scriptures in all languages

outliers.note: Alone identifies the flying angel with an institution of his own lifetime, the British and Foreign Bible Society, and lists the languages into which it had already put the Scriptures — the most datable identification anywhere in the chapter.

Alone records that Origen took the eternal gospel to be another book still to be written, and alone builds an argument from the missing article and from the noun occurring nowhere else in this writer.

themes: having the everlasting gospel to preach
fear God, and give glory to him
the hour of his judgment is come

8.pericope_label: And there followed another angel, saying, Babylon is fallen, is fallen, that great city, because she made all nations drink of the wine of the wrath of her fornication.

schools.summary: Proceed by abstraction rather than identification: the literal Babylon was chiefly remembered by the Hebrews as the power that invaded the holy land, ruined the temple, reduced the country to a province and carried the people into captivity, so that the name became an emblem of everything haughty and oppressive and especially of whatever persecutes the church, and the word must here denote some later power resembling it in those characteristics. Or refuse to fix it to one age at all: pagan Rome was Babylon to the seer, papal Rome to a later age, and Babylon has reared palaces on the Seine and the Thames as well as the Tiber and the Bosphorus, so that she is an emblem of principles all nations have accepted in some measure and in whose fall all will be more or less involved. Say plainly that Rome is meant, and add the circumstance that explains the veil, since a prisoner on Patmos could speak his mind only by such symbolism. Hear the doubled verb as a dirge announcing the certainty of the fall, prefer the English participial rendering as more musical than the literal one, and trace the echo to Isaiah, noting that one Greek witness there has the perfect. Derive the phrase that follows from Jeremiah's oracle against Babylon, and picture Rome as the great courtesan who intoxicates and beguiles the nations while the cup of wrath stands full for her and her paramours. Add that the principles of the gospel must undermine the world-power, so that the fall of some Babylon principle has almost always followed an age of spiritual revival.

Date her: Rome commenced Babylon when it commenced the great city, that is when it swallowed the Grecian monarchy and its fragments and so obtained dominion over Jerusalem some sixty years before the nativity; her spiritual greatness began in the fifth century and increased from age to age, and will reach its height just before the overthrow. Note that the epithet great is added wherever the name occurs. Read the whole as a parallel: what Babylon was to the Israel of old, Rome has been to the literal and the spiritual Israel alike, so that as the liberty of the ancient Jews was bound up with the fall of the Babylonish empire, the liberty of God's people waits on the fall of Rome. Identify the fornication with idolatry, the invocation of saints and angels, the worship of images and human traditions, holding that fleshly fornication is joined to the spiritual abundantly; and observe pointedly that the making of the nations drink is ascribed not to the beast but to Babylon herself. Report also that Rome is called Babylon in the rabbinical writings, ask which Rome is meant, and answer only that some parts of the description apply best to the pagan one. Explain the image from a practice rather than a text: impure women gave love potions to those they wished to bind to their will, intoxicating in nature, inflaming the blood and disturbing the intellect, so that the wine of wrath is the envenomed cup given by such women.

Take the second angel for another set of gospel ministers following immediately on the first, who proclaim the fall which the preaching of the everlasting gospel will have brought about. Offer the candidates in sequence: the Waldenses and Albigenses, who gave a great blow to Babylon and laid a foundation for her ruin; then Luther and the reformers of his times, who gave her a deadly blow so that she has been falling ever since; but settle on a body of ministers still to come, in the spiritual reign of Christ, who will not merely declare her fall certain and near at hand but will live to see and proclaim her actual fall.

sides.position: Some later power resembling the literal Babylon in being proud, oppressive and a persecutor of the church
Rome, though whether pagan or papal is unsettled; some parts of the description apply best to the pagan
Rome plainly, the symbolism being how a prisoner on Patmos could speak his mind
Not one age or city: pagan Rome to the seer, papal Rome later, and she has reared palaces on the Seine, the Thames and the Bosphorus
When it commenced the great city, swallowing the Grecian monarchy and gaining dominion over Jerusalem some sixty years before the nativity
The question is misplaced; Babylon names principles which all nations have accepted in some measure
The Waldenses and Albigenses, or Luther and the reformers, or better a body of ministers still to come who will live to see her actual fall
A second angel who follows on the first and interprets him in part
The angel whose proclamation follows the gospel angel, since the principles of the gospel undermine the world-power

outliers.note: Alone dates the transformation precisely, holding that Rome became Babylon when it swallowed the Grecian monarchy and gained dominion over Jerusalem about sixty years before the nativity, its spiritual greatness beginning in the fifth century.
Alone refuses to fix Babylon to any single city or age, extending her to the Seine and the Thames as well as the Tiber and the Bosphorus and making her a set of principles rather than a place.

themes: Babylon is fallen, is fallen, that great city
the wine of the wrath of her fornication

9.pericope_label: And the third angel followed them, saying with a loud voice, If any man worship the beast and his image, and receive his mark in his forehead, or in his hand, The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name. Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus.

schools.summary: Take the image from the practice of holding out poison to a condemned man to drink and die, and explain unmixed as undiluted with water, that is at full strength, so that the punishment is unmitigated. Find in the Greek a bold and powerful oxymoron, since the participle means mixed and the adjective means unmixed, so that the phrase reads the mixed unmixed: the wine is unmixed with water yet mixed with spices to make it stronger still. Distinguish the two nouns for anger that stand side by side elsewhere, one vehement fury and the other settled indignation, and say the white heat held back through the ages will be turned loose. On the duration, be guarded about what the words strictly prove: the clause affirms only that the smoke of their torment ascends, which does not by itself assert that the individual sufferings are eternal, though it is such language as would be used on that supposition and can hardly be explained otherwise. Or move the question onto moral ground, reading the restlessness as the natural consequence of sin, which is first embraced as a delight and soon becomes an inexorable tyrant compelling men along habits they loathe while they long for them, so that there is a destiny of unrest in all sin. Note that the phrase for having no rest is the very language used earlier of the living creatures praising God, and that those who desert Christ for Caesar become the victims of a remorse that never dies or sleeps. On the closing verse, correct the rendering so that it runs here is the patience of the saints who keep, not here are they that keep, and note the anacoluthon.

Read the sentence as retributive: having drunk the intoxicating wine of spiritual fornication they now drink the wine of God's wrath, an allusion to the poisoned cup certain criminals were obliged to drink, on which speedy death followed. Hear in fire and brimstone an allusion to the punishment of Sodom, and take the angels and the Lamb as instruments employed in the destruction rather than mere spectators. Call this the most terrible threatening in all Scripture, and observe that God arms his servants against the fear of the beast by a greater fear; then ask whether no real anger is implied in all this, and exclaim at what even wise men will assert in order to serve a hypothesis. Pray that neither writer nor reader may ever try the strict literal eternity of this torment. On the patience, suggest that the word sometimes means the reward of perseverance rather than the virtue, so that the verse promises blessedness to those who die for the testimony; and say that the patience is seen in suffering all things rather than receive this mark.

Take the punishment as just, since those who drank of the wine of Rome's fornication now drink of the wine of God's wrath, and note that it is usual in Scripture to express punishment by the wine cup of his fury and the suffering of it by drinking; add that wine of wrath is a phrase the Jewish writers use. On the smoke, say plainly that there will be no end to the torment, and cite the Jewish phrase about the smoke of hell filling the eyes of the wicked in the world to come. Then read the patience of the saints as that which they have been patiently waiting for, namely the destruction of antichrist, which being now come, patience will have its perfect work.

debates.question: Does the ascending smoke prove the torment endless?

sides.position: There will be no end to it; the misery is called everlasting fire and everlasting destruction
The clause affirms only that the smoke ascends, which does not by itself assert that individual sufferings are eternal, though it is such language as would be used on that supposition
The unrest is the natural consequence of sin, which becomes an inexorable tyrant; there is a destiny of unrest in all sin
God grant we may never try the strict literal eternity of this torment
Undiluted with water, that is at full strength, so the punishment is unmitigated
A bold oxymoron — the mixed unmixed: unmixed with water yet mixed with spices to make it stronger still

debates.question: What is the patience of the saints?

sides.position: Either that those who show it prove themselves God's children, or that the disclosure about the persecutors' end is designed to sustain them
Sometimes the word means the reward of perseverance rather than the virtue, so the verse promises blessedness to those who die for the testimony
The readiness to wait and endure to the end; the rendering should be the patience of the saints who keep, not here are they that keep
That which they have waited for, namely the destruction of antichrist, now come

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse against a theological opponent, asking whether no real anger is implied in all this and exclaiming at what even wise men will assert to serve a hypothesis — and alone recoils from the duration, praying that neither writer nor reader may ever try its strict literal eternity.

Alone distinguishes what the words assert from what they presuppose, granting that the clause affirms only that the smoke ascends and not that individual sufferings are eternal, while holding that it can hardly be explained on any other supposition.

themes: the wine of the wrath of God, poured out without mixture
the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever
here is the patience of the saints

13.pericope_label: And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.

schools.summary: Suggest that the seer had been recording what he saw and is now told to record what he heard, and offer the verse as evidence that the book was written as the disclosures were made rather than afterwards from memory. Say that the meditation is broken by the command, and that this beatitude for the Christian dead goes further than what the apostle had written to the Thessalonians and Corinthians. Note that we are not told whose voice speaks, and insist that the blessing covers not only martyrs but all who die in happy union and fellowship with their Lord. On the words from henceforth, find them a difficulty and offer the state of trouble just described as the reason, the righteous being happy in being taken from the evil to come; add a second use, that they may console mourners in an age whose unbelief writes farewell for ever over its graves — or attach the phrase instead to those who die in the Lord. Make the works that follow works of faith and labours of love, even the giving of a cup of cold water in Christ's name, following with them into the presence of their Lord. Then draw the distinction the Greek makes: they rest from their toils and wearinesses but not from their activities, since those follow with them, heaven being not a place of idleness but of the highest form of spiritual service, so that growth cut short here can be utilised there.

Note that the command to write had already been given for the whole book, so that wherever it is repeated it marks something peculiarly observable; guess that the voice belonged to a departed saint; and observe that the word is heard most seasonably when the beast is at the height of his power and fury. Set the saying beside its pagan analogues: happy are the dead is a proverb frequently met with in the Greek and Roman poets, and quote the Odyssey, where the shipwrecked man calls thrice and four times happy those who fell at Troy, and then the Latin imitation, where the hero's limbs loosen with cold and he stretches both palms to the stars with the same cry. Divide the happiness of the Christian dead into two things the pagan proverb reaches only in part: they do not see the evil coming on the world and are exempt from further suffering, and they actually enjoy blessedness. Say that the works do not go before to procure admittance into the mansions of joy but follow when admittance is given, and that what follows is the fruit of the works, each one's peculiar works. Mark the contrast sharply: no pain and no purgatory follows, the more laborious the life the sweeter the rest, and this state is the opposite of those two verses earlier who have no rest day or night.

Value the prophecy for coming down from heaven and not from men, which makes it of certain truth and great authority, and for being preserved by writing as a matter of record to which the people of God may have recourse for support and comfort. Describe those who are blessed as such as die in the cause of Christ, or rather die in a state of vital union with him, being found in Christ when death comes. Then demonstrate the blessedness twice over: they are blessed in their rest, resting from sin, temptation, sorrow and persecution; and blessed in their recompence, since their works do not go before them as their title or price of purchase but follow them as the evidence of having lived and died in the Lord.

debates.question: What do the words from henceforth attach to?

sides.position: To the blessing, and the reason is the trouble just described: the righteous are happy in being taken from the evil to come
To the blessing, on two grounds: they escape the approaching calamities and already enjoy so near an approach to glory
Probably to those who die in the Lord, giving comfort to those facing persecution and death

debates.question: In what sense do their works follow them?

sides.position: Not as their title or price of purchase, but as evidence of having lived and died in the Lord
They do not go before to procure admittance but follow when admittance is given; what follows is the fruit of the works
As works of faith and labours of love following with them into their Lord's presence
They rest from toils and wearinesses but not from activities, since heaven is not idleness but the highest form of spiritual service

debates.question: Does the verse bear on the manner of the book's composition?

sides.position: It may be cited as proof that the book was written as the heavenly disclosures were made, and not afterwards from memory
The command was given at first for the whole book, so its repetition marks something peculiarly observable

outliers.note: Alone sets the beatitude beside its pagan analogues, quoting the Odyssey on those thrice happy who fell at Troy and the Latin imitation of it, and then marking the two ways the Christian blessing exceeds the proverb.

Alone presses the distinction between the toils they rest from and the activities that follow with them, concluding that heaven is not a place of idleness but of the highest form of spiritual service, so that growth cut short here can be utilised there.

themes: blessed are the dead which die in the Lord
they may rest from their labours

14.pericope_label: And I looked, and behold a white cloud, and upon the cloud one sat like unto the Son of man, having on his head a golden crown, and in his hand a sharp sickle. And another angel came out of the temple, crying with a loud voice to him that sat on the cloud, Thrust in thy sickle, and reap: for the time is come for thee to reap; for the harvest of the earth is ripe. And he that sat on the cloud thrust in his sickle on the earth; and the earth was reaped. And another angel came out of the temple which is in heaven, he also having a sharp sickle. And another angel came out from the altar, which had power over fire; and cried with a loud cry to him that had the sharp sickle, saying, Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe. And the angel thrust in his sickle into the earth, and gathered the vine of the earth, and cast it into the great winepress of the wrath of God. And the winepress was trodden without the city, and blood came out of the winepress, even unto the horse bridles, by the space of a thousand and six hundred furlongs.

schools.summary: Build the identification of the figure on the cloud from converging marks — the cloud, the title son of man, the crown, the general resemblance to the opening vision of the book — and find a designed reference to Daniel. Distinguish the crown from the diadems worn later, this being a wreath of victory, and call the cloud a familiar object in Mediterranean lands. Number the angels as they come, the fourth crying to the reaper, the fifth carrying the second sickle, the sixth calling for the vintage, and insist on the direction of the first command: it is not the angel's order but the Father's, borne by the angel to the Son, which agrees with the whole New Testament representation that the Messiah is subordinate in the work given him to do. Note the urgency in the aorist imperatives, and take the verb rendered ripe as meaning dried up or withered rather than over-ripe. On the angel from the altar, give the alternatives and their consequences: if it is the altar of burnt offering we are reminded of the blood of the martyrs, if the altar of incense then of the prayers of the saints. On the measured distance, compute it as two hundred miles and treat it as a lake of blood standing for a great slaughter without pressing the figure; allow that the distance covers the length of the land, but judge it more likely that the metaphor is worked out with the exuberance of apocalyptic symbolism. Note that a winepress stood in the vineyard rather than in a city, that this was the usual place, and that a prophet had made the valley of Jehoshaphat the scene of the slaughter of God's enemies.

Read the crown as a token of victory and regal power, and say that harvest and vintage were frequent images among the ancient prophets for the destruction and excision of nations. Identify the angel from the altar with the one mentioned earlier who stood by the altar of burnt-offering with authority over its fire to offer the incense that represents the prayers of the saints. Take the winepress as trodden by the Son of God and the city as Jerusalem, which the first readers would have understood without being told. Then find a modern coincidence in the measured distance, reporting that the papal state extends from Rome to the Po, two hundred Italian miles, which make exactly sixteen hundred furlongs, and call the correspondence surprising and worthy of deep regard; supply also the Jewish hyperbole that when Hadrian besieged a certain city he slew so many that the horses waded in blood up to their mouths. Mark the depth of the blood as deep at its first flowing, and the distance as reaching through the whole land.

Separate the objects of the two images. Warnings and judgments not having produced reformation, the sins of the nations are filled up and they become ripe for judgment, represented by a harvest — an emblem also used of the gathering of the righteous when they are ripe for heaven, so that the wheat of the earth is gathered into Christ's garner. Then by a vintage: the enemies of Christ and his church are not destroyed until by their sin they are ripe for ruin, and then he will spare them no longer. Make the winepress the wrath of God, some terrible calamity, probably the sword shedding the blood of the wicked; and close on the observation that the patience of God towards sinners is the greatest miracle in the world, but though lasting it will not be everlasting, and ripeness in sin is a sure proof of judgment at hand.

Identify the figure on the cloud by elimination: not some great prince who encouraged the Reformation among his subjects, nor an angel in human shape, nor Martin Luther as others have said, but Christ himself, described by his form, his seat, what he has on his head and what he holds in his hand. On the angel from the temple, reject in turn the Holy Spirit, who is never called an angel, and the souls under the altar, and prefer either the mighty angels who will descend with Christ as reapers or a set of gospel ministers who will know by the signs of the time that the harvest is come. Report without endorsing the interpretation that made these two angels Thomas Cromwell and Archbishop Cranmer, and the vintage the dissolution of the religious houses and the disposal of abbey lands. Mention the suggestion that the olive presses outside Jerusalem gave Gethsemane its name, and note that the beloved city is the new Jerusalem, into which none of the wicked will enter.

debates.question: Who sits on the white cloud?

sides.position: Christ himself — not a prince who favoured the Reformation, nor an angel in human shape, nor Martin Luther as some have said
Christ, on the converging evidence of the cloud, the title, the crown and the resemblance to the opening vision

debates.question: Whose is the command to thrust in the sickle?

sides.position: Not the angel's but the Father's, borne by the angel to the Son, since the Messiah is subordinate in the work given him
The angel urges Christ, the urgency lying in the aorist imperatives

debates.question: Which altar does the sixth angel come from?

sides.position: The altar of burnt offering, which recalls the blood of the martyrs — or the altar of incense, which recalls the prayers of the saints
The altar of burnt-offering, where the angel of an earlier chapter had authority over the fire to offer incense
Both earlier scenes are in view: the souls beneath the altar and the angel who flung the burning ashes earthward
Not the Holy Spirit and not the souls under the altar, but the mighty angels who will descend with Christ, or a set of gospel ministers

debates.question: What are the sixteen hundred furlongs?

sides.position: Two hundred miles, a lake of blood standing for a great slaughter, the figure not to be pressed
The whole land of Palestine
The extent of the papal state, from Rome to the Po — a surprising coincidence worthy of deep regard
It does cover the length of the land, but more likely the metaphor is worked out with the exuberance of apocalyptic symbolism

outliers.note: Alone reports the interpretation that identified the two angels of the vintage with Thomas Cromwell and Archbishop Cranmer and the vintage itself with the dissolution of the religious houses — and reports it without endorsing it.

Alone finds a literal modern measurement in the sixteen hundred furlongs, matching them to the extent of the papal state from Rome to the Po and calling the coincidence surprising and worthy of deep regard.
